transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-05-18 16:00 UTC | Duration: 72 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Lucia Gomez (Redwood Platform), Tom Sato (Redwood SRE); Samir Patel (Bluehaven ML Eng), Dana Liu (Bluehaven Infra Lead), Priya Nair (CTO), Ethan Ross (Data Scientist)

Summary: deep dive on GPU runtime profiling; kernel selection heuristics; differences observed between TRT-LLM path and v L L M style runtime; CUDA Graph warmup / amortization; KV-cache behavior under continuous batching; quantization impact (int8/4-bit) on kernel choice; on-prem network/VPC implications for multi-GPU inference.

00:00 Maya: okay, good afternoon everyone, thanks for making time. we'll do a deep dive. we have about 70 minutes. hope that's still okay.
00:12 Priya: yes that's great, want to focus on throughput and predictable p99 latencies for our contact summarization pipelines.
00:21 Arjun: quick agenda: 1) kernel selection and dynamic routing, 2) CUDA Graph profiling and warmup, 3) KV cache and continuous batching effects, 4) quantization tradeoffs, 5) on-prem/VPC multi-GPU network notes, then Qs and action items.
00:36 Dana: quick note, infra is a 4x A100 NVLink box in our prod lab, and we do 2k concurrent streams with short prompt lengths (~256 tokens) but occasional spikes to 4k.
00:49 Arjun: perfect, that explains some of the behaviors we saw in your perf traces.
01:05 Samir: we ran a side-by-side: TRT-LLM pipeline vs an open v L L M build; we saw lower median with TRT but p99s were worse when we had many short requests.
01:20 Arjun: yeah that's a common pattern. TensorRT path picks fused kernels that are great for long sequences and full utilization, but for many short queries the kernel launch and serialization can dominate unless you use CUDA Graph warmup and persistent CUDA streams.
01:40 Maya: could you elaborate on what we mean by kernel selection heuristics?
01:44 Arjun: sure. runtime has a kernel selector that chooses between: 1) dense attention kernels (fused matmul+softmax), 2) split attention with cuBLAS-backed matmul, 3) Triton-custom fused kernels (for TRT-LLM), and 4) fallback generic kernels (our fallback path). The selector uses heuristics based on sequence length distribution, batch size, and current GPU occupancy. We also consider quantization mode — int8 kernels route differently.
02:10 Tom: and memory fragmentation matters. if large KV caches are pinned in GPU memory, it changes how many warps can be scheduled which causes the runtime to pick lower-parallelism kernels.
02:24 Ethan: we noticed token generation stalls sometimes after a big spike — feels like memory pressure or GC.
02:31 Lucia: that's often fragmentation or suboptimal allocator behavior. our runtime attempts to defrag and provision pools but we saw fragmentation with variable sequence lengths. we log block utilization to help tune pool sizes.
03:02 Dana: on the TRT side, we tried TRT-LLM with CUDA Graphs baked for the 256 token path. median improved, but tail increased on our mixed workload. Why?
03:15 Arjun: CUDA Graphs give great low-overhead replay but they're most efficient when the execution path is identical between runs. Mixed workloads trigger graph re-generation or fallback to non-graph path; that recompile/regeneration is expensive. Also TRT fused kernels sometimes have conditional paths that aren't graph-friendly. If you have many different prompt lengths, you either pre-bake graphs for common lengths or use dynamic graph capture which has overhead.
03:44 Samir: we captured nvprof traces — attaching in the shared sheet — and it showed spikes at specific steps labeled "kernel_launch 0x7f" and lots of small kernel launches between tokens.
03:56 Arjun: small kernel launches are killers in high-req-per-second regimes. continuous batching helps: we maintain a small batching window (3–10 ms) which merges short requests, reduces kernel launch count, and allows using higher-throughput fused kernels. There's a tradeoff: added latency vs throughput.
04:20 Priya: latency SLO is 120ms p95, p99 we want <400ms. Can continuous batching meet that?
04:30 Maya: depends on traffic surface. if you have sustained short requests, batching with 5–10ms helps. we also do route-by-policy: high-tier customers get single-request fast-path (lower batching) on dedicated pools.
04:45 Dana: what about KV cache behavior? we rely heavily on caching prefixes for customer sessions. we saw cache miss storms on restarts.
04:53 Arjun: KV cache layout is key. TRT-LLM's optimization sometimes reorganizes KV into contiguous buffers for fast attention; v L L M style runtimes often keep dictionary-of-tensors which can be more flexible. When you have many concurrent sessions with different prefix lengths, you get fragmentation. Our runtime supports per-session pooling and an eviction policy optimized for prefix reuse — we also expose metrics for cache hit ratio and compactness.
05:30 Samir: is there a break-even token length where TRT path becomes strictly better?
05:36 Arjun: empirically we see TRT path win for sequences >1024 tokens at moderate batch sizes (>8) on A100. For short sequences (<512) and small batch sizes, the lighter non-fused kernels or v L L M path can be faster due to lower kernel launch overhead. But quantization changes this curve.
05:56 Ethan: speaking of quantization — we tried int8 and 4-bit funnel quantization. int8 gave speedups but introduced some coherence loss in summaries. 4-bit was faster for large batches but jittery. Thoughts?
06:12 Arjun: quantization affects kernel selection because some kernels are specialized for int8 or int4 (packing/packing/unpacking). Also, calibration and per-channel scales matter. For int8, TRT-LLM often uses optimized INT8 GEMM; for 4-bit we sometimes use fused decompression kernels that add CPU/GPU overhead. There's also non-determinism in mixed-precision accumulation which affects p99.
06:40 Priya: how do you recommend we validate quality regression with quant?
06:45 Maya: run evals on a held-out prompt set, track exact-match/rouge/embedding cosine. Redwood Optimize has an eval harness; SEs can help run A/Bs with deterministic seeds.
06:53 Dana: back to CUDA Graphs — you mentioned warmup/ amortization. How many warmup runs until the graph overhead pays off?
07:02 Arjun: depends on kernel complexity and graph size. For small kernels (~couple of ms), amortization happens after ~100–500 captures. For larger graphs (multi-stage decoding with large KV), you might need fewer captures. But the key cost is capture+replay management; if graphs are invalidated frequently due to variable dims, it doesn't pay. We recommend: pre-bake graphs for the 90th percentile sequence lengths and fallback otherwise.
07:36 Samir: we could pre-bake for 128/256/512/1024 and route based on length. That might cover 95% of traffic.
07:44 Arjun: exactly — routing by length + policy is what we call kernel routing table. The runtime can maintain multiple graph pools and a fallback interpreter path. We also monitor graph churn rate.
08:00 Tom: networking note for on-prem/VPC: NVLink helps intra-box multi-GPU but across nodes you need efficient RDMA; NICs (Mellanox 100G+) and correct NCCL tuning are critical. We saw serialization if NCCL rings are suboptimal or TCP fallback occurs.
08:20 Dana: we're planning multi-node scaling. any gotchas for KV cache across nodes?
08:26 Arjun: distributed KV cache is tricky. You can partition sessions by owner and keep KV local to a GPU to avoid cross-node fetches. Or use an external KV store with high-speed RDMA reads, but that adds latency. Redwood's routing can pin sessions to GPUs/nodes and do warm handovers to avoid cross-node miss storms.
08:46 Samir: what about inference on lower-memory cards like L40s or RTX-class for cost saving?
08:52 Arjun: then quantization + sequence-slicing become necessary. You might need offload (CPU/GPU split) for KV, or recompute KV for longer sequences. Kernel selection shifts toward streaming kernels that operate with smaller working sets. We also support partitioned attention kernels in our runtime.
09:10 Priya: curious about measurement: what should we capture in traces to make analysis fruitful?
09:15 Arjun: capture: 1) per-kernel launch timestamps, names, durations, occupancy; 2) CUDA Graph capture/replay events; 3) memory alloc/free traces and fragmentation stats; 4) KV hit/miss counters; 5) batch merging stats and latency buckets; 6) NIC send/recv for multi-node; 7) GPU metrics: SM utilization, l2/cache, memory bandwidth. CUPTI + nvprof + Nsight Systems combined is great. We'll share a capture checklist.
09:48 Samir: we've been using Nsight and a few flamegraphs. we'll share the traces.
09:55 Arjun: perfect. also consider instrumenting the runtime's internal route decisions (why we picked kernel X) — those logs are very actionable.
10:05 Maya: quick demo excerpt — Arjun, can you walk through a specific trace we saw?
10:10 Arjun: yes, pulled up the row from the shared sheet (link pasted in chat). in this trace you can see repeated small kernels ~0.2ms each instead of 1 fused kernel at ~1.6ms. lots of launches at steps 12–20. those came from per-token attention kernels in the fallback path. The fallback path is safe but many tiny kernels cost context-switch overhead.
10:38 Ethan: that aligns with our observation of p99 spikes during bursts.
10:42 Arjun: resolution options: 1) enable short-request batching (3–7ms), 2) pre-bake graphs for common lengths to hit fused kernels, 3) force fused kernels by setting threshold parameters (risk of slightly higher memory).
11:02 Samir: about the threshold parameters — would that increase memory usage significantly?
11:07 Arjun: yes, fused kernels can require larger contiguous buffers (for packed KV). we saw ~10–20% extra GPU memory usage for some models on A100. If you're memory constrained, may need quantization or offload.
11:25 Dana: and GC behavior? we've seen fragmentation on frequent small session churn.
11:30 Lucia: we recommend session pooling and reuse; when sessions terminate we don't immediately free GPU blocks but return them to a fast pool. also background defrag tasks run during low-util windows. tuning pool sizes to your session churn is essential.
11:50 Priya: okay high-level ask: can Redwood run a targeted POC on our infra with our workload?
11:55 Maya: yes — typical POC: we run onsite or remote benchmarks, deploy a Private instance (customer-managed) or Dedicated pool, run pre-baked graph + fallback configs, simulate production traffic (mix of 256/1024/4k), and compare p50/p95/p99 and cost.
12:10 Dana: security questions: if we run Private on-prem does Redwood need outbound access?
12:16 Maya: Private can be air-gapped; control-plane handshake can be via customer proxy or offline bundle. we do recommend connectivity for patching but it's optional. we'll send the security checklist.
12:28 Priya: any notes on E2E observability for these perf experiments?
12:32 Tom: we capture token-level tracing, per-request timeline, and we tag each trace with kernel decisions. we provide dashboards showing graph hit ratio, cache hit ratio, kernel churn, and memory fragmentation over time.
12:50 Samir: on the benchmarking front: what about model variants? we have small and large versions; how to pick?
12:56 Arjun: route by cost/latency: small model for high-concurrency short prompts; large model for long form generation. we also support auto-fallback to cheaper models when capacity constrained. In Dedicated you can pin variants to different GPU classes.
13:12 Ethan: one more — for CUDA Graphs is there a recommended capture cadence for code changes?
13:17 Arjun: whenever you update tokenizer, model layers, or quantization, re-capture. Also on driver or CUDA upgrades. Small changes invalidating graphs happen often; incorporate graph capture into your CI if you rely heavily on pre-baked graphs.
13:34 Maya: ok let's do a quick recap and next steps.
13:40 Maya: recap: we will share CUPTI traces and a capture checklist, Bluehaven will upload sample workloads, SE will run a POC with pre-baked graphs for 128/256/512/1024, and we'll test quantization A/Bs for int8 vs 4-bit on your A100 box.
13:58 Priya: sounds good.
14:05 Maya: action items recorded in calendar and I'll email timeline. thanks everyone.

Notes / artifacts referenced: shared perf spreadsheet: https://drive.enterprise/bluehaven-perf/trace-20250518.csv; POC doc: https://redwood.app/POC-templates/llm-gpu-profiling.pdf
